latin: AD Glastoniensium monachorum, de Josepho Arimathæensi et ejus sociis, traditiones nunc venio: quas etsi Normannorum adventu antiquiores non existimem, et posteriorum temporum superstitionem plane redoleant; tamen qualescunque sunt, ex Guilielmi Malmesburiensis de antiquitate Glastoniensis ecclesiæ libello exhibere visum est.
mt_english: I now come to the traditions of the monks of Glastonbury concerning Joseph of Arimathea and his companions. Although I do not consider them older than the arrival of the Normans, and they clearly smack of the superstition of later times, nevertheless, such as they are, I have decided to present them from William of Malmesbury's book "On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury".
baker_ref: GLASTONBURY TRADITIONS concerning JOSEPH OF ARIMATHEA (Translated from Ussher's ‘ Antiquities ' Ch. ii) I NOW Come to the traditions of the Monks of Glaston concerning Joseph of Arimathea and his companions: which, although I do not esteem them more ancient than the coming of the Normans and are plainly redolent of the superstition of later times, yet, of whatever quality they are, it seemed well to me to set them out from the book of William of Malmesbury on the " Antiquity of the Church of Glaston."

latin: Sic igitur ille, præmissa præfatione ad Henricum Blesensem, Henrici I. regis ex Adela sorore nepotem, Wintoniensem tum episcopum et Glastoniensem abbatem, archæologiam suam ab apostolicis exorditur temporibus.
mt_english: Thus, having prefixed a preface to Henry of Blois, nephew of King Henry I by his sister Adela, and at that time bishop of Winchester and abbot of Glastonbury, he begins his ancient history from apostolic times.
baker_ref: Thus, then, with a preliminary preface to Henry of Blois- nephew to King Henry I, by his sister Adela-then Bishop of Winchester and Abbot of Glaston, he commences his archæology from Apostolic times.

latin: " Post Dominicæ resurrectionis gloriam, ascensionisque triumphum, ac Spiritus paracliti de supernis missionem (qui discipulorum corda temporalis pœnæ adhuc formidine trepidantia replevit, scientiam omnium linguarum tribuendo) erant omnes credentes simul cum mulieribus, et Maria matre Jesu, ut Lucas narrat evangelista: et verbum Dei disseminabatur, crescebatque numerus credentium quotidie; eratque omnibus cor unum et anima una. Invidiæ ergo facibus accensi sacerdotes Judæorum cum Pharisæis et Scribis, concitaverunt persecutionem in Ecclesia, interficiendo protomartyrem Stephanum, et fere a finibus suis omnes procul pellentes. Hac igitur persecutionis procella sæviente, dispersi credentes petierunt diversa regna terrarum a Domino sibi delegata, verbum salutis gentibus propinando. Sanctus autem Philippus, ut testatur Frecul-
mt_english: "After the glory of the Lord's resurrection, and the triumph of his ascension, and the sending of the Paraclete Spirit from on high (who filled the hearts of the disciples, still trembling with the fear of temporal punishment, by bestowing the knowledge of all languages), all the believers were together with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, as Luke the evangelist narrates: and the word of God was spread abroad, and the number of believers grew daily; and they all had one heart and one soul. Therefore, inflamed by the torches of envy, the priests of the Jews, with the Pharisees and Scribes, stirred up a persecution in the Church, killing the protomartyr Stephen, and driving almost everyone far from their borders. While this storm of persecution raged, therefore, the dispersed believers sought the diverse kingdoms of the earth delegated to them by the Lord, dispensing the word of salvation to the peoples. But Saint Philip, as Frecul- testifies..."
baker_ref: "After the glory of the Lord's resurrection, and the triumph of His ascension, and the sending of the Spirit, the Comforter from on high (who filled the disciples ' hearts till then trembling through fear of earthly punishment, by imparting to them a knowledge of all tongues ), all the believers were together with the women, and Mary the Mother of Jesus, as Luke the Evangelist relates: and the Word of God was spread, and the number of the believers increased daily; and in all there was one heart and one mind. Then the priests of the Jews, with the Pharisees and Scribes, inflamed with the fires of envy, stirred up a persecution in the Church, by slaying the protomartyr, Stephan, and driving afar nearly all from their borders. "Whilst, therefore, this storm of persecution was raging, the scattered believers sought divers kingdoms of the earth, chosen by the Lord for Himself, in order to deliver the Word of Salvation to the nations. Now St. Philip, as Freculphus testifieth in his second book, Chapter IV, coming into the region of the Franks in order to preach, converted many to the faith and baptized them. Thereupon, purposing to spread Christ's Word, he chose twelve from among his disciples, and sent them into Britain to preach the Gospel of the Word of Life: over whom he placed in authority, it is said, his dearest friend, Joseph of Arimathea, who buried the Lord. "Coming therefore into Britain in the 63rd year from the Incarnation of the Lord, the 15th from the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, they preached with boldness the faith of Christ. But the barbarian king with his people, hearing such novel and unaccustomed things, absolutely refused to agree with their preaching, neither did he wish to change the traditions of his ancestors; yet, because they were come from far, and he observed the sobriety of their mode of life, he granted them a certain island, surrounded by woods, thickets and marshes, called by its inhabitants Ynswitrin, on the confines of his territories, in which to dwell.

latin: Postea etiam alii duo reges pagani successive comperta vitæ eorum sanctimonia, unicuique eorum unam portionem terræ concesserunt; ac ad petitionem ipsorum, secundum morem gentis, brevi dictas duodecim hidas confirmaverunt. Unde et duodecim hidæ per eos adhuc, ut creditur, nomen sortiuntur."
mt_english: Afterward, two other pagan kings in succession, having discovered the sanctity of their lives, granted each of them a portion of land; and at their request, according to the custom of the people, they confirmed the said twelve hides by a brief. Whence also the twelve hides still, as it is believed, derive their name from them."
baker_ref: Moreover, afterwards, two other pagan kings observing their pious mode of life successively granted to each of them a portion of land; and at their request, confirmed to them by a writing (brevi) the said XII portions after the manner of the nation. Whence, as it is believed, the Twelve Hides take their name from them to this day.

latin: " Prædicti itaque sancti in eodem deserto conversantes, post pusillum temporis visione archangeli Gabrielis admoniti sunt ecclesiam in honore sanctæ Dei genitricis et virginis Mariæ, in loco cœlitus eis demonstrato construere.
mt_english: "And so the aforesaid saints, dwelling in that same desert, after a short time were instructed by a vision of the archangel Gabriel to build a church in honor of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, in a place revealed to them from heaven.
baker_ref: "And thus the said saints, dwelling together in this desert place, were in a very short time inspired by a vision of the Archangel Gabriel to build a church in honour of the Holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary in a place divinely revealed to them, who quick to obey the Divine precepts, completed a certain chapel according to what had been shewn them, fashioning its walls below, throughout its circumference, of twisted wattles, in the XXXIst year after the Passion of the Lord, and the XVth after the a literis.

latin: Qui divinis præceptis non segniter obedientes, secundum quod eis fuerat ostensum, quandam capellam, inferius per circuitum virgis torquatis muros perficientes, consummaverunt in anno post passionem Domini tricesimo primo, post assumptionem gloriosæ virginis decimo quinto, et deformi quidem schemate, sed Dei multipliciter adornatam virtute. Et cum hæc in hac regione prima fuerit; ampliori eam dignitate Dei filius insignivit, ipsam videlicet in honore suæ matris dedicando. Duodecim igitur sancti sæpius memorati, in eodem loco Deo et beatæ virgini devota exhibentes obsequia; vigiliis, jejuniis et orationibus vacantes, ejusdem virginis auxilio ac visione (ut credi pium est) in omnibus necessitatibus refocillabantur. Hæc autem ita se habere, tum ex charta beati Patricii, tum ex scriptis seniorum cognoscimus.”
mt_english: Promptly obeying the divine commands, according to what had been shown to them, they completed a certain chapel, constructing its lower walls all around with twisted twigs, in the thirty-first year after the passion of the Lord, and the fifteenth after the assumption of the glorious Virgin, unshapely indeed in design, but manifoldly adorned by the power of God. And since this was the first in this region, the Son of God distinguished it with greater dignity, namely by dedicating it in honor of his mother. Therefore the twelve frequently mentioned saints, offering devout service to God and the blessed Virgin in that same place, devoting themselves to vigils, fasts, and prayers, were refreshed in all their necessities by the help and vision of the same Virgin (as it is pious to believe). Moreover, I know that these things are so, both from the charter of the blessed Patrick and from the writings of the elders."
baker_ref: Assumption of the Glorious Virgin, rude, it is true, in form, but richly adorned with the power of God. "And as this was the first in that region, the Son of God distinguished it with greater dignity by dedicating it in honour of His Mother. "Thereupon the XII saints-so frequently mentioned, paying devout homage in that same spot to God and the Blessed Virgin; devoting themselves to vigils, fasts, and prayers, were constantly sustained ( as it is pious to believe ) in all their needs by the same Virgin's help and presence. "That these things are so we learn both from the Charter of the Blessed Patrick and from the Writings ofthe Elders."

latin: Addit præterea Malmesburiensis, ad Glastoniensis ecclesiæ antiquitatem comprobandam, et sequens testimonium: “Monachus quidam Glastoniæ, Godefridus nomine, (de cujus epistola hoc capitulum assumpsimus) tempore Henrici Blesensis, abbatis Glastoniensis, cum in pago Parisiacensi apud sanctum Dionysium moraretur; senior quidam ex monachis interrogavit eum: quo genus, unde domo? Respondit, Normannum, e Britanniæ monasterio quod Glastingeia dicitur, monachum. Papæ, inquit, an adhuc stat illa perpetuæ virginis et misericordiæ matris vetusta ecclesia? Stat, inquit. Tum ille lepido attactu caput G. Glastoniensis demulcens, diu silentio suspensum tenuit, ac sic demum ora resolvit; hæc gloriosissimi martyris Dionysii ecclesia, et illa de qua te asseris, eandem privilegii dignitatem habent: ista in Gallia, illa in Britannia uno eodem tempore exortæ, a summo et magno pontifice consecratæ. Uno tamen gradu illa supereminet: Roma etenim secunda vocatur.”
mt_english: William of Malmesbury adds, moreover, to prove the antiquity of the church of Glastonbury, the following testimony as well: "A certain monk of Glastonbury, Godfrey by name (from whose letter I have taken this chapter), in the time of Henry of Blois, abbot of Glastonbury, while he was staying in the district of Paris at Saint-Denis, was asked by a certain elder among the monks: of what race are you, and where is your home? He answered that he was a Norman, a monk from a monastery in Britain which is called Glastonbury. 'Indeed,' he said, 'does that ancient church of the perpetual virgin and mother of mercy still stand?' 'It stands,' he said. Then he, stroking the head of Godfrey of Glastonbury with a gentle touch, held him in suspense for a long time in silence, and at last opened his mouth thus: 'This church of the most glorious martyr Denis, and that one from which you assert yourself to be, have the same dignity of privilege: this one in Gaul, that one in Britain, having arisen at one and the same time, were consecrated by the highest and great pontiff. Yet that one excels by one degree: for it is called a second Rome.'"
baker_ref: Later, Malmesbury adds, inproof of the antiquity of the Church ofGlaston, the following evidence also: "In the time of Henry of Blois, Abbot of Glastonia, acertain monk of Glastonia, Godefride by name (from whose epistle we have taken this extract ),when he was staying atSt. Denys, inthe district of Paris; acertain Elder of the monks enquired of him: of what race he was, and where he dwelt? He replied, aNorman, amonk of amonastery inBritain called Glastingeia. How strange,' said he, ΙΟ 'doth that most ancient church of the Perpetual Virgin and Mother of Mercy still endure?' 'It doth,' replied he. Thereupon he, with gentle touch caressing the head of Godefride of Glaston, kept silence for a long while and at length broke forth thus: "This Church of the most glorious Martyr Denys, and that of which thou speakest, possess the same dignity of privilege: this in Gaul, that in Britain, founded at one and the same time and consecrated by the Most High and Mighty Pontiff. Nevertheless, in one respect that one is supereminent: since it is called Rome the Second '."

latin: Refert Cæsar Baronius ex actis Mariæ Magdalenæ et sociorum, dispersione facta post mortem Stephani, “Lazarum, Mariam Magdalenam, Martham, et Marcellam pedissequam, in quos Judæi majori odio exardescebant, non tantum Hierosolymis pulsos esse, sed una cum Maximino discipulo, navi absque remigio impositos, in certum periculum mari fuisse creditos: quos divina providentia Massiliam tradunt appulisse.” Additque ex historia Anglorum, quæ manuscripta habetur in bibliotheca Vaticana, sed (quod ille tacet, et nos suo loco patefaciemus) nostris temporibus scripta, “comitem ejusdem discriminis Josephum ab Arimathæa nobilem decurionem; quem tradunt ex Gallia in Britanniam navigasse, illicque post prædicatum evangelium diem clausisse extremum.” In PseudoDextri quoque chronico, ad annum Christi XLVIII. similiter legimus; “ Hierosolymitani Judæi vehementer infensi B. Lazaro, Magdalenæ, Marthæ, Marcellæ, Maximino, Josepho ab Arimathia nobili decurioni, et aliis plurimis ; navi sine remigio velisque, ac sine gubernatore eos imponunt, et exulare mandant : qui per vastum mare divinitus delati, ad Massiliensem portum incolumes appellunt.” Et in fragmento Helecæ attributo; “Fama est, Magdalenam Lazari sororem, cum Lazaro, Maximo atque Chelidonio, Marcella, Josepho ab Arimathia, venisse in Galliam Aquitanicam; ibique prædicasse Domini Jesu sanctum evangelium: ut docent luculenter Gallorum historiæ, et est traditio ubique satis recepta illius regionis.” Quod autem de Philippi in Galliis apostolatu habet Freculphus a Malmesburiensi citatus; ex Isidori libro de patribus utriusque Testamenti ad verbum expressit. Apud utrumque enim legimus, Philippum Gallis prædicasse Christum, “ barbarasque gentes, vicinasque tenebris, et tumenti oceano conjunctas, ad scientiæ lucem, fideique portum deduxisse.” Neque hic mihi Baronii conjectura placet, Isidori ista a Gallis nostris ad Galatas Asiaticos traducentis : multoque minus, nuperi operum Isidori editoris, Jacobi Breulii temeritas, Galatis pro Gallis in ipso textu, sine ulla veteris lectionis commemoratione, reponentis.
mt_english: Caesar Baronius reports from the acts of Mary Magdalene and her companions, that when the dispersion occurred after the death of Stephen, "Lazarus, Mary Magdalene, Martha, and Marcella the handmaid, against whom the Jews burned with greater hatred, were not only driven from Jerusalem, but together with the disciple Maximinus, having been placed in a ship without oars, were entrusted to the sea in certain danger: who, they relate, were driven by divine providence to Marseille." And he adds from a history of the English, which is kept in manuscript in the Vatican Library, but (which he passes over in silence, and I will reveal in its proper place) was written in our own times, "that Joseph of Arimathea, the noble decurion, was a companion in the same peril; who, they relate, sailed from Gaul into Britain, and there, after preaching the gospel, ended his last day." In the chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter, too, at the year of Christ 48, I read similarly: "The Jews of Jerusalem, violently hostile to the blessed Lazarus, Magdalene, Martha, Marcella, Maximinus, Joseph of Arimathea the noble decurion, and many others, place them in a ship without oars or sails, and without a pilot, and order them into exile: who, carried by divine power through the vast sea, land safely at the port of Marseille." And in a fragment attributed to Heleca: "The report is that Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, with Lazarus, Maximus and Chelidonius, Marcella, and Joseph of Arimathea, came into Aquitanian Gaul; and there preached the holy gospel of the Lord Jesus: as the histories of the Gauls clearly teach, and it is a tradition sufficiently received everywhere in that region." But what Freculf, cited by William of Malmesbury, has concerning the apostolate of Philip in the Gauls, he expressed word for word from Isidore's book "On the Fathers of Both Testaments". For in both I read that Philip preached Christ to the Gauls, "and led the barbarous peoples, neighboring on darkness and joined to the swelling ocean, to the light of knowledge and the port of faith." Nor does the conjecture of Baronius please me here, transferring these words of Isidore from our Gauls to the Asiatic Galatians: and much less the rashness of the recent editor of Isidore's works, Jacques du Breul, replacing Gauls with Galatians in the text itself, without any mention of the old reading.
baker_ref: Caesar Baronius quotes from the Acts of Mary Magdalene and her Companions on the dispersion after the death of Stephan: "That Lazarus, Mary Magdalene, Martha and Marcella, their attendant, against whom the Jews displayed the greater hatred, were not only driven from Jerusalem but, in company with Maximinus the disciple, were put into a boat without oars and were consigned to the sure peril of the sea: who by divine providence, they say, reached Marseilles." b Baron. Annal., tom 1., ann. 35, sec. 5., Vid. Petrum de Natalibus, lib. 6., cap. 124. Melchiorem Inchofer, de veritate Epistolae B. Mariae and Messanenses., cap. 13; et Fran. Bosquet., Eccles Gallican. hist., lib. 1., sec. 3. II And he adds from the " History of England, ” which MS. is preserved in the Vatican Library, but (of which he says nothing, and we in his stead shall disclose ) written in our times, "that their companion in this crisis was Joseph of Arimathea, the noble decurion, who, they relate, sailed out of Gaul into Britain and, thereafter, preaching the gospel, ended his days." In the "Chronicle of Pseudo -Dexter," also, we similarly read that in the year of Christ 48: "The Jews of Jerusalem being violently hostile to the Blessed Lazarus, Magdalene, Martha, Marcella, Maximin, Joseph of Arimathea, the noble decurion, and many others, put them in a ship without oars or sails and without a rudder and ordered them to live in banishment: who, being divinely carried by the mighty ocean, reached the port of Marseilles uninjured.” And in a fragment attributed to Heleca: "It is said that Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, with Lazarus, Maximus and Chelidonius, Marcella and Joseph of Arimathea, came into Aquitanian Gaul and there preached the Holy Gospel of the Lord Jesus, as the histories of Gaul clearly teach and is the generally accepted tradition of that region." Moreover, that which Freculphus -cited by Malmesbury -holds concerning the apostleship of Philip in Gaul is expressed word for word in the book of Isidore concerning the Fathers of each Testament. C For in each we read that Philip preached Christ to the Gauls,"and that he led nations, barbarous and near to darkness and bordering on the swelling ocean, to the light of knowledge and to the gate of faith." I am not at all satisfied here with the conjecture of Baroniusd in transferring the statements of Isidore from our Gauls to the Galatians of Asia; much less with the temerity of a recent editor of the works of Isidore, Jacobus Breulius, in substituting Galatians for Gauls in the text itself without any reference to the ancient reading.

latin: Nam præterquam quod Isidorus in hoc ipso opere, capite secundo et octogesimo et in officio Toletano, quod Gothicum et Mozarabum vulgo appellatur : itemque Julianus Toletanus archiepiscopus in Nahum prophetam scribens, et Beda (vel quicunque author fuit collectaneorum et florum ad calcem tertii tomi operum ipsius adjectorum) Philippo Galliam assignant: idemque “ Gallis prædicavisse Christum” legitur, in libello de festis apostolorum, qui in Hieronymiano martyrologio manuscripto habetur, ex quo pleraque omnia in librum suum de patribus novi Testamenti transcripsit Isidorus: illa barbararum gentium oceano conjunctarum mentio, Europæos Gallos, non GalloGræcos ab Isidoro intellectos esse satis evincit.
mt_english: For besides the fact that Isidore in this very work, chapter 82, and in the Toledan office, which is commonly called Gothic and Mozarabic; and likewise Julian, archbishop of Toledo, writing on the prophet Nahum, and Bede (or whoever was the author of the collections and excerpts appended to the end of the third volume of his works) assign Gaul to Philip; and that he is read to have "preached Christ to the Gauls" in the little book "On the Feasts of the Apostles", which is contained in the manuscript "Hieronymian Martyrology", from which Isidore transcribed almost everything into his book "On the Fathers of the New Testament": that mention of barbarian peoples bordering the ocean sufficiently proves that Isidore meant the European Gauls, not the Galatians.
baker_ref: For, besides, Isidore in this very work in the 82nd Chapter and in the Liturgy (officio ) of Toledo, which is commonly called Gothic and Mozarabic; also Julian Archbishop of Toledo writing on the Prophet Nahum, ' and Bede (or whoever was the author of the "Collections and Flowers " placed at the foot of the 3rd tome of his works), assign Gaul to Philip. d Baron., tom. 1., ann. 44., sec. 32, et eum secutus, Jacobus Valdesius, de dignitate reg. Hisp., Cap. 6., sec. 56. e Offic. Mozar. in festo S. Jac., Tomo 2, Auctarii bibliother patrum, edit. Paris, ann. 1610, col. 1659, in Hymno de S. Jacobo quem inde desumptum commentario suo in Dextri chronicon inseruit Franc. Bivarius, p. 86. f ibid., col. 205. And the same man is said "To have preached Christ to the Gauls " in the book on the "Feasts of the Apostles ": which is found in the MS. "Martyrology of Hieronymus," from which Isidore transcribed nearly everything into his book on the Fathers of the New Testament; this mention of the barbarian nations adjacent to the Ocean sufficiently shews that they were European Gauls and not the Gallo -Greeks claimed by Isidore.

latin: Quod vero Josephi Arimathæensis opera in gentibus Britannicis ad fidem perducendis Philippus usus fuerit, id totum ex Glastoniensium monachorum lacunis haustum est: a quibus et barbari illi manarunt versiculi, ex chronicis quibusdam de rege Arvirago agentibus citati: Intrat Avalloniam duodena caterva virorum; Flos Arimathææ Joseph est primus eorum.
mt_english: But the claim that Philip used the assistance of Joseph of Arimathea in bringing the British peoples to the faith is entirely drawn from the pools of the Glastonbury monks: from whom also those barbarous little verses flowed, cited from certain chronicles dealing with King Arviragus: "A band of twelve men enters Avalon; Joseph, the flower of Arimathea, is the first of them."
baker_ref: Now, as for Philip having used the aid of Joseph of Arimathea in bringing the people of Britain to the faith, this is to be drawn from the wells of knowledge (lacunis) of the Monks of Glaston from which indeed have originated these rude verses quoted out of certain chronicles concerning King Arviragus: "There enters Avallonia a band of twelve men; Of these the flower and chief is Joseph of Arimathea.

latin: Josephes ex Joseph genitus patrem comitatur; His aliisque decem jus Glastoniæ propriatur.
mt_english: "Josephes, born of Joseph, accompanies his father; to these and the other ten the right of Glastonbury is appropriated."
baker_ref: Josephes the son of Joseph accompanies his Father: To them and to the other ten the freedom of Glaston is granted."

baker_ref: And these from others of equal grace: "Philip ordered Joseph to cross with his companions. To the land of Britain to preach the divine Word.

latin: Habetur et hodie Welliæ in ædibus D. Thomæ Hugonis equitis aurati, tabula ænea, columnæ Glastoniensis ecclesiæ olim affixa: cui incisum legitur: “ Anno post passionem Domini XXXI. duodecim sancti, ex quibus Joseph ab Arimathia primus erat, huc venerunt, qui Ecclesiam hujus regni primam in hoc loco construxerunt, quam Christus in honorem suæ matris et locum pro eorum sepultura præsentialiter dedicavit.” Est etiam penes nobilissimum virum, D. Guilielmum Howardum, Thomæ Norfolciæ Ducis filium, ingens tabula, Glastonienses antiquitates undique conquisitas complectens : in qua, inter alia fabulosissima, et ista legimus : “ Joseph ab Arimathia beati Philippi apostoli discipulatui se contulit, atque ejus salubri doctrina aﬄuenter refertus et ab ipso cum filio suo Josepho baptizatus est. Postea vero a beato Johanne apostolo ipsi prædicationi Ephesiorum insudante, beatæ perpetuæque virginis Mariæ paranymphus delegatus est : ejusdem quoque gloriosæ virginis venerandæ assumptioni cum beato Philippo cæterisque discipulis interfuit, atque ea quæ de Domino Jesu Christo atque ejus gloriosa genitrice Maria audierat et viderat instanter per diversas regiones prædicans, ac multos convertens et baptizans ; tandem decimo quinto post eandem gloriosam assumptionem anno, cum memorato filio suo Josepho ad sanctum Philippum in Gallias venit. Ac deinde secundum quod legitur in libro qui dicitur Graal, Joseph ab Arimathia, qui dominum sepelivit, baptizatus a beato Philippo apostolo venit in majorem Britanniam, sibi et semini ejus promissam, cum uxore, et filio Josephe nomine, quem ipse Salvator noster in civitate Saraz prius in episcopum consecraverat.”
mt_english: There is also kept today at Wells, in the house of Sir Thomas Hughes, knight, a bronze tablet, formerly affixed to a column of the Glastonbury church: on which is read the inscription: "In the 31st year after the passion of the Lord, twelve saints, of whom Joseph of Arimathea was the first, came here, who constructed the first church of this kingdom in this place, which Christ personally dedicated in honor of his mother and as a place for their burial." There is also in the possession of the most noble man, Lord William Howard, son of Thomas Duke of Norfolk, a huge tablet, comprising Glastonbury antiquities collected from all sides: in which, among other most fabulous things, I read these as well: "Joseph of Arimathea betook himself to the discipleship of the blessed apostle Philip, and being abundantly filled with his wholesome doctrine, was baptized by him along with his son Josephes. But afterwards, by the blessed apostle John, who was himself laboring in the preaching to the Ephesians, he was delegated as the paranymph of the blessed and perpetual virgin Mary: he was also present at the venerable assumption of the same glorious virgin with the blessed Philip and the other disciples, and earnestly preaching through various regions those things which he had heard and seen concerning the Lord Jesus Christ and his glorious mother Mary, and converting and baptizing many; at length, in the fifteenth year after the same glorious assumption, he came with his aforementioned son Josephes to Saint Philip in Gaul. And then, according to what is read in the book which is called the Graal, Joseph of Arimathea, who buried the Lord, having been baptized by the blessed apostle Philip, came into greater Britain, promised to him and his seed, with his wife, and a son named Josephes, whom our Savior himself had previously consecrated as bishop in the city of Sarras."
baker_ref: Is first Church of this Kingdom, in this place which Christ at that time dedicated to the honour of His Mother and as a place for their burial." Furthermore, there is in the possession of the Most Noble D. William Howard, son of Thomas, Duke of Norfolk, a remarkable tablet comprising the antiquities of Glaston, collected from all quarters, inwhich, among other very fabulous matters, we read also the following: "Joseph of Arimathea attached himself tothe disciples of the Blessed Apostle Philip and was abundantly filled with his wholesome doctrine, and,with his son Joseph, baptized by him. "Afterwards, moreover, he was appointed by the Blessed Apostle John, toiling exclusively for the instruction of the Ephesians, asattendant (paranymphus ) ofthe Blessed and Perpetual Virgin Mary: and was also, with the Blessed Philip and the other disciples, present atthe Assumption of the Glorious and Adorable Virgin and, constantly preaching through divers regions those things which he had heard and seen touching both the Lord Jesus Christ and His Glorious Mother Mary, converting and baptizing many, he came atlength inthe XVth year after that glorious Assumption, with his aforementioned son Joseph toSaint Philip inGaul. And thereafter, according to what is read in the Book which is called 'Graal,' Joseph of Arimathea who buried the Lord, baptized by the Blessed Apostle Philip came into Greater Britain, promised to him and to his seed, together with his wife and his son, Joseph by name, whom the Saviour Himself had previously consecrated to be bishop in the fellowship of Saraz (in civitate Saraz ).”

latin: Sequuntur deinde portenta illa, quæ in vita Josephi refert Capgravius ex eodem nugacissimo libro, qui sanctum Graal appellatur, cujus auctor Guilielmo Malmesburiensi paulo videtur fuisse posterior ; licet ab Helinando Cluniacensi, Frigidi montis in Gallia monacho, ad annum salutis DCCXX. referatur. Sic enim ille in chronico, a Vincentio Bellovacensi citato : “ Hoc,” inquit, “ tempore in Britannia cuidam eremitæ monstrata est mirabilis quædam visio per angelum, de sancto Joseph decurione nobili, qui corpus Domini deposuit de cruce, et de catino illo vel de paropside, in quo Dominus cœnavit cum discipulis suis, de quo ab eodem eremita descripta est historia, quæ dicitur de Gradali. Gradalis autem vel Gradale Gallice dicitur scutella lata, et aliquantulum profunda, in qua pretiosæ dapes cum suo jure divitibus solent apponi, gradatim unus morsellus post alium in diversis ordinibus; et dicitur vulgari nomine Graal, quia grata et acceptabilis est, in ea comedenti, tum propter continens, quia forte argentea est, vel de alia pretiosa materia; tum propter contentum, id est, ordinem multiplicem dapum pretiosarum. Hanc hiſtoriam Latine scriptam inveniri non potui: sed tantum Gallice scripta habetur a quibusdam proceribus, nec facile (ut aiunt) inveniri potest.”
mt_english: Then follow those marvels which Capgrave relates in the life of Joseph from that same most trifling book which is called the Holy Grail, whose author seems to have been slightly later than William of Malmesbury; although it is assigned to the year of salvation 720 by Helinand the Cluniac, a monk of Froidmont in Gaul. For thus he says in his chronicle, cited by Vincent of Beauvais: "At this time," he says, "a certain marvelous vision was shown by an angel to a hermit in Britain, concerning Saint Joseph, the noble decurion, who took down the Lord's body from the cross, and concerning that bowl or dish in which the Lord dined with his disciples, about which a history was written by that same hermit, which is called the history of the Grail. Now a Gradalis or Gradale in French means a wide and somewhat deep dish, in which precious meats with their broth are usually served to the rich, step by step, one morsel after another in various courses; and it is called by the common name Graal, because it is pleasing and acceptable to the one eating from it, both on account of the container, because perhaps it is silver or of another precious material, and on account of the contents, that is, the manifold succession of precious meats. I have not been able to find this history written in Latin: but it is kept written only in French by certain nobles, nor can it easily be found (as they say)."
baker_ref: Next follow those wonderful stories in the life of Joseph which Capgrave relates in his most frivolous book, which is called the " Holy Graal,' of which the author seems to have been a little later than William of Malmesbury: although it is referred by Helinandus Cluniacensis, a monk of Mons Frigidus in Gaul to the year of grace DCCXX. For thus he writes in the Chronicle, quoted by Vincentius Bellovacensis: < "At this time," he says, " in Britain a certain marvellous vision was shewn by an Angel to a certain hermit, concerning the holy Joseph, the noble Decurion, who took down the body of the Lord from the Cross, and concerning the vessel or dish out of which the Lord supped with His disciples, of which a history was written by this same hermit, and is called ' Concerning the Gradalis.' Now, the Graal, or in Gallic Gradale, is said to be a salver, broad and somewhat deep, in which the costly feast together with the appointed condiments is wont to be placed before the rich, one morsel after another in different layers: and it is called by the common name of Graal, because it is pleasing and acceptable to him eating therefrom; as well on account of the container, which is perhaps of silver or some other precious metal, as of the contents, that is the manifold variety of the precious feast. I have not been able to find this history written in Latin; but, written in Gallic only, it is possessed by certain nobles, nor, so they say, can it easily be found.

latin: Multa vero inde in fabulosa regis Arthuri acta, lingua Anglicana a se edita, transtulit Thomas Malorius: qui Sangreal vocem hic usurpat, ad sanguinis realis notionem proxime accedentem; partem enim pretiosissimi sanguinis Servatoris nostri repoſitum hic fuisse fingit: sive in cruce eﬀusi, sive ex suprema Chriſti cœna reservati: de qua Stephanus Forcatulus: “ Britanni sacræ illius cœnæ pignus ac testimonium secum attulisse Josephum commemorant: nempe catinum sanctissimis convivis appositum, diutissime in magna ceremonia, tanquam pignus quoddam securitatis Britannicæ; non aliter atque Trojanum Palladium.” Hæc ille: de aucta etiam a Josepho vetere magia Britannica eﬀatum non minus a ratione quam a religione remotum postea adjiciens: “ Auxit prodigiosos ritus Josephus Arimathæus, advena Britanniæ plauſsbilis; qui de Solomonis fonte artem hauserat. Fuit namque hic sapiens rex imbutus divinitus secretiore sapientia: incantationes composuit, quibus morbi pellerentur, et dæmones fugarentur, non redituri.”
mt_english: Thomas Malory indeed translated many things from there into the fabulous acts of King Arthur, published by him in the English language: who here uses the word Sangreal, coming very close to the notion of 'real blood'; for he imagines that a part of the most precious blood of our Savior was deposited here, whether shed on the cross, or reserved from Christ's last supper. Concerning which Stephen Forcatulus says: 'The Britons record that Joseph brought with him a pledge and testimony of that sacred supper: namely, the dish served to the most holy guests, kept for a very long time with great ceremony, as a certain pledge of British security, not otherwise than the Trojan Palladium.' Thus he writes, afterwards adding a statement about the ancient British magic having been increased by Joseph, a statement no less removed from reason than from religion: 'Joseph of Arimathea, an acceptable stranger to Britain, increased the prodigious rites; who had drawn his art from the fountain of Solomon. For this wise king was divinely imbued with a more secret wisdom: he composed incantations, by which diseases might be driven away, and demons put to flight, never to return.'

latin: De duodecim discipulis a B. Philippo in Britanniam missis, Malmesburiensis quidam monachus in eulogii sui libro secundo hunc in modum meminit: “ Anno Incarnationis Domini LXIII. et assumptionis beatæ virginis Mariæ XV. duodecim discipuli venerunt in Britanniam majorem, missi a beato Philippo apostolo ad verbum Dei ibidem prædicandum: quorum primus fuit Joseph ab Arimathia, qui Jesum Christum sepelivit. Quibus rex Arviragus, licet paganus, ne ulterius laborarent, duodecim hidas terræ eis contulit in insula Avalloniæ, quæ nunc dicitur Glastonia. In quo loco ecclesiam in honore beatæ virginis per admonitionem S. Michaelis archangeli, de virgis torquatis muros facientes, construxerunt."
mt_english: Concerning the twelve disciples sent into Britain by the blessed Philip, a certain monk of Malmesbury records in the second book of his eulogy in this manner: 'In the year of the Lord's Incarnation 63, and the 15th of the assumption of the blessed virgin Mary, twelve disciples came into greater Britain, sent by the blessed apostle Philip to preach the word of God there: the first of whom was Joseph of Arimathea, who buried Jesus Christ. To whom King Arviragus, although a pagan, lest they should labor further, granted twelve hides of land in the island of Avalon, which is now called Glastonbury. In which place they constructed a church in honor of the blessed virgin by the admonition of St. Michael the archangel, making the walls of twisted twigs.'
baker_ref: Of the twelve disciples sent by the Blessed Philip into Britain, a certain monk of Malmesbury, in the second book of his "Eulogy," makes mention in this manner: "In the LXIII year from the Lord's Incarnation and the XV from the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary twelve disciples came into Greater Britain sent thither by the Blessed Apostle Philip to preach the word of God: of whom the chief was Joseph of Arimathea who buried Jesus Christ. On whom the King Arviragus, although a pagan, in order that they might toil no longer, conferred XII hides of land in the Isle of Avalon which is now called Glastonia. n Id., ibid; pag. 1002. Vid. Jacob Valdesium, de dignitate Hispaniae, Cap. 16, sec. 12. Ex Josepho, lib. 8, Antiquit. Judaic, cap, 2, In which place they constructed a church in honour of the Blessed Virgin. by direction of the Holy Archangel Michael, making the walls of twisted wattles."

latin: In chronico quoque Glastoniensi anno MCCLIX. exarato, scriptum legimus: "Anno ab Incarnatione LXIII. discipuli sanctorum Philippi et Jacobi apostolorum venerunt in Britanniam: a quibus primum oratorium in insula Avalloniæ, in honore S. Mariæ fuit constructum, in anno post assumptionem ejusdem quinto decimo." Et in ali0, a monacho cœnobii S. Augustini Cantuariensis anno MCCCCVI. conscripto: "Rex Yna fuit primus fundator monasterii Glastoniensis. Monachi tamen ibidem aliam prætendunt fundationem a rege Arvirago (filio Kimbelini regis Britonum, in cujus tempore Christus Jesus de Maria virgine natus fuit) et quod ab Arthuro rege dotatum fuit pluribus possessionibus." Item in libro de prærogativis et dignitatibus ordinem monasticum concernentibus, qui a Thoma Walsinghamio scriptus putatur: "S. Philippus apostolus Jesu Christi misit in Britanniam duodecim prædicatores, quorum primus et præcipuus fuit Joseph ab Arimathia, qui Christum sepelivit. Qui Glasconiam venientes, acceperunt possessionem hidarum duodecim, ab Arvirago nobili rege Britanniæ, adhuc paganicis erroribus involuto. Hi per Gabrielis archangeli admonitionem, ecclesiam in honore sanctæ Dei genetricis Mariæ construxerunt anno post passionem Domini tricesimo primo."
mt_english: Also in the Glastonbury chronicle written in the year 1259, I read: "In the year 63 from the Incarnation, the disciples of the holy apostles Philip and James came to Britain: by whom the first oratory in the isle of Avalon was constructed in honor of St. Mary, in the fifteenth year after her assumption." And in another, written by a monk of the monastery of St. Augustine at Canterbury in the year 1406: "King Yna was the first founder of the monastery of Glastonbury. The monks there, however, claim another foundation by King Arviragus (son of Kimbelinus, king of the Britons, in whose time Jesus Christ was born of the Virgin Mary) and that it was endowed with many possessions by King Arthur." Likewise in the book "On the Prerogatives and Dignities Concerning the Monastic Order", which is thought to have been written by Thomas Walsingham: "St. Philip, the apostle of Jesus Christ, sent twelve preachers into Britain, of whom the first and chief was Joseph of Arimathea, who buried Christ. Coming to Glastonbury, they received possession of twelve hides from Arviragus, the noble king of Britain, who was still entangled in pagan errors. These men, by the admonition of the archangel Gabriel, constructed a church in honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God, in the thirty-first year after the passion of the Lord."
baker_ref: In the " Chronicle of Glaston," also, entered in the year MCCLIX, we find written: "In the year LXIII from the Incarnation, disciples of the Holy Apostles Philip and James came into Britain: by whom the first oratory was built in the Isle of Avalon in honour of S. Mary, in the XV year after her Assumption." And in another, " written by a monk of the community of S. Augustine of Canterbury in the year MCCCCVI: "King Yna was the first founder of the Monastery of Glaston. Nevertheless the monks there allege another foundation by King Arviragus (son of Kimbeline, King of the Britons, in whose time Christ Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary) and which was endowed with numerous possessions by King Arthur." Also in a Book of the " Prerogatives and Dignities," concerning the monastic Order, which is thought to be written by Thomas Walsingham: "S. Philip, the Apostle of Jesus Christ, sent XII preachers into Britain, of whom the first and chiefest was Joseph of Arimathea who buried P MS. in bibliotheca Cottoniana. 9 MS. M. Roberti Haraei. Christ. Who, coming to Glastonia, received possession of xii hides from Arviragus, the noble King of Britain, though still steeped in pagan errors. These by the admonition of the Archangel Gabriel, built a Church in honour of the Holy Mary Mother of God in the xxxi year after the Lord's Passion."

latin: Johannes Tinmuthensis, ex Glastoniensis monasterii libris, ita rem narrat: "Ex quo apostoli in regiones diversas erant divisi ad prædicandum verbum vitæ, sanctus Philippus apostolus regionem Franciæ cum suis discipulis sortitus est: de quibus misit in Britanniam duodecim (quorum primus erat Joseph ab Arimathia, qui et Dominum sepelivit) anno ab incarnatione Domini sexagesimo tertio, et ab assumptione sanctæ Mariæ quinto decimo : quibus duodecim hidæ ab Arvirago paganicis erroribus decepto concessæ erant. Qui ibidem Deo servientes, per Gabrielis archangeli admonitionem; ecclesiam in honore sanctæ Dei genetricis Mariæ construxerant. Cumque fidem Christi constanter prædicarent, rex barbarus cum gente sua tam nova audiens et inconsueta, omnino prædicationi eorum consentire renuebat, nec paternas traditiones commutare volebat: quia tamen de longe venerant, ad petitionem eorum quandam insulam sylvis paludibusque circumdatam ad inhabitandum concessit. Erat enim portio illa duodecim hidarum, et quandam capellam (ut præmittitur) ex virgis torquatis construxerunt anno post passionem Domini XXXI.” Hæc Johannes Tinmuthensis, in sanctilogio Britanniæ, et ejus exscriptor Johannes Capgravius in nova legenda Angliæ, sed prudenter præmisso hoc prologo. “ Quæ inferius digesta sunt, apud Glastoniam ex libris monasterii illius excerpsi: quæ si veritatem sapiant, lectoris arbitrio relinquo.” Et hoc ad extremum subjecto epilogo. “ Ego vero in præscriptis et dubiis, et in sequentibus nonnullis, authoritatem discutiendi et definiendi mihi non præsumo: sed tanquam relator simplex, quæ in diversis libris et locis cum laboribus et difficultate sedulus indagator reperire potui, ardua peritis ventilanda relinquens, sine invidia communico.”
mt_english: John of Tynemouth, from the books of the monastery of Glastonbury, narrates the matter thus: "From the time when the apostles were divided into different regions to preach the word of life, the holy apostle Philip was allotted the region of France with his disciples: of whom he sent twelve into Britain (the first of whom was Joseph of Arimathea, who also buried the Lord) in the sixty-third year from the incarnation of the Lord, and the fifteenth from the assumption of St. Mary: to whom twelve hides were granted by Arviragus, who was deceived by pagan errors. Serving God there, by the admonition of the archangel Gabriel, they constructed a church in honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God. And when they constantly preached the faith of Christ, the barbarian king with his people, hearing such new and unaccustomed things, altogether refused to consent to their preaching, nor did he wish to change his paternal traditions: however, because they had come from afar, at their petition he granted them a certain island surrounded by woods and marshes to inhabit. For that portion was of twelve hides, and they constructed a certain chapel (as is premised) out of twisted twigs in the 31st year after the passion of the Lord." These things John of Tynemouth states in his "Sanctilogium Britanniae", and his transcriber John Capgrave in the "Nova Legenda Angliae", but having prudently premised this prologue: "The things which are digested below, I excerpted at Glastonbury from the books of that monastery: whether they taste of the truth, I leave to the judgment of the reader." And with this epilogue appended at the end: "But I do not presume for myself the authority of discussing and defining the aforementioned and doubtful matters, and some of the following ones: but as a simple relator, leaving the difficult matters to be examined by experts, I communicate without envy what I, as a diligent investigator, could find in various books and places with labor and difficulty."
baker_ref: John Tinmuth thus narrates the matter from the books of the Monastery of Glaston: "After that the Apostles had dispersed into divers regions in order to preach the Word of Life, the Holy Apostle Philip, with his disciples, was allotted the region of the Franks: of whom he sent xii into Britain (Joseph of Arimathea who buried the Lord being the chief) in the sixtythird year from the Lord's Incarnation, and the fifteenth from the Assumption of S. Mary; to whom were granted xii hides by Arviragus though blinded by pagan errors. There, serving God, they erected by direction of the Archangel Gabriel, a Church in honour of Saint Mary the Mother of God. And though they steadfastly preached the faith of Christ, the barbarian King with his people, hearing such new and unaccustomed things altogether refused to accept their preaching nor was he willing to depart from the traditions of his fathers: nevertheless, because (translated ). Almost the same words are found in the Cottonian MS., where various prophecies of Merlin and others are collected together. they had come from afar, he acceded to their petition to be allowed to inhabit a certain island surrounded by woods and marshes. That portion in truth was xii hides and they built there (as has been premised ) a chapel out of twisted wattles in the year XXXI from the Lord's Passion," Thus Johns Tinmuth in his "History of the British Saints " and John Capgrave, who copied from him, in his " New Legends of England, " but prudently with this preface: "That which is set out below, I have selected at Glaston from the books of that Monastery which as to whether they savour of truth I leave to the judgment of the reader." And, towards the end this comment is appended: "I, however, do not take upon myself the authority of discussing or determining what is doubtful in the foregoing or in some which follow: but as a simple relator I communicate without distinction those things which, as an assiduous searcher, I have with labour and difficulty been able to meet with in divers books and places, leaving the difficulties to the judgment of experts.

latin: Polydorus Vergilius, vir naris emunctioris, sublatis crassioribus illis monachorum fabulamentis, historiam hanc ita proponit. “ Joseph ille, qui, teste Matthæo evangelista, ab Arimathæa civitate oriundus, Christi corpus sepeliverat, sive casu, sive consilio, ita volente Deo, cum non parvo comitatu, in Britanniam venit: ubi tam ipse, quam ejus socii, cum de evangelio prædicarent, atque dogma Christi sedulo docerent, multi per hæc ad veram pietatem traducti, salutiferaque fruge imbuti, baptizati sunt. Isti viri certe divino spiritu aﬄati, cum a rege parum terræ ad inhabitandum (proxime Welliam oppidum, circiter millia passuum quatuor) dono accepissent, ibi novæ religionis prima jecerunt fundamenta, ubi hodie est templum magnificum cœnobiumque monasticæ familiæ D. Benedicti ordinis nobile. Loco nomen est Glasconia. Hæc omnino Christianæ pietatis in Britannia extitere primordia; quam deinde Lucius rex, sicut paulo post dicemus, prope extinctam baptismi fonte sublatus mirabiliter accendit, pieque adauxit. Nam Gildas testis est, Britannos jam inde ab initio orti evangelii, Christianam recepisse religionem."
mt_english: Polydore Vergil, a man of finer discernment, having removed those grosser fables of the monks, sets forth this history as follows: "That Joseph, who, as the evangelist Matthew testifies, originating from the city of Arimathea, had buried the body of Christ, whether by chance or by design, God so willing, came into Britain with a considerable retinue; where, when both he and his companions preached the gospel and diligently taught the doctrine of Christ, many were drawn by these things to true piety, imbued with saving fruit, and baptized. These men, certainly inspired by the divine spirit, having received as a gift from the king a small piece of land to inhabit (near the town of Wells, about four miles away), laid the first foundations of the new religion there, where today there is a magnificent church and a noble monastery of the monastic family of the order of St. Benedict. The name of the place is Glastonbury. These were altogether the beginnings of Christian piety in Britain; which King Lucius, as I will say shortly, when it was nearly extinguished, having been raised from the baptismal font, miraculously rekindled and piously increased. For Gildas is a witness that the Britons had received the Christian religion right from the beginning of the risen gospel."

For Gildas is witness that the British received the Christian religion from the very beginning of the rise of the Gospel."

latin: Hæc Polydorus. Et ante eum Richardus Lepidus Bartholinus. "Nec me præterit," inquit, "Josephum ab Arimathea, cum a Judæis nequiter in carcerem ductus fuisset, et a Deo Optimo Maximo miraculose liberatum taliter ut nusquam postea in Judæa visum fuisse. Nam, ut annalium scriptores prodiderunt, in Britanniam transmigravit; ibique et cultum Christi docuit, et multa sui monumenta in valle Avilonis, quæ adhuc visuntur, reliquit."
mt_english: Thus Polydore. And before him, Richardus Lepidus Bartholinus. "It does not escape me," he says, "that Joseph of Arimathea, after he had been wickedly imprisoned by the Jews, was miraculously delivered by God Most High in such a way that he was never afterwards seen in Judea. For, as the writers of annals have recorded, he migrated to Britain; and there he both taught the worship of Christ, and left many monuments of himself in the valley of Avalon, which are still seen."
baker_ref: Thus Polydore. And before him Richardus Lepidus Bartholinus: "Nor do I forget," says he, "that Joseph of Arimathea, when he was shamefully imprisoned by the Jews and so miraculously liberated by Almighty God, was nowhere seen again in Judea. For, as the writers of the annals shewed, he migrated into Britain; and there he both taught the worship of Christ and left many memorials of himself in the Vale of Avalon, which can there be seen.”

latin: Eadem etiam de Josephi adventu refert Thomas Scropus, Dromorensis quondam in Hibernia episcopus, capite septimo libri quem de Carmelitani ordinis antiquitate scripsit. Et Thomas Harfeldius, in breviario regum Anglorum: ubi Faganum et Duvianum (sive Deruvianum) Lucii regis temporibus in insula Avalloniæ "antiquam ecclesiam a discipulis Christi fabricatam reperisse dicit, cum antiquis scriptis, qualiter sanctis apostolis ad prædicandum dispersis, sanctus Philippus in Franciam veniens duodecim ex suis discipulis in Britanniam misit; quibus et Joseph ab Arimathia præfecit." Et extat sane adhuc magni nostri Patricii nomine, a Glastoniensibus monachis conficta epistola (charta ea est B. Patricii, a Malmesburiensi superius citata) in qua de origine ecclesiæ quæ Anglo-Saxonibus Ealdcirc, id est, vetusta ecclesia dicta est, ita ille disserens introducitur. “Ostenderunt mihi fratres scripta sanctorum Phagani et Deruviani: in quibus continebatur, quod duodecim discipuli sanctorum Philippi et Jacobi ipsam vetustam ecclesiam construxerant in honore prælibatæ advocatricis nostræ, B. Mariæ virginis, per doctrinamentum beati archangeli Gabrielis. Insuper et quod Dominus eandem ecclesiam cœlitus in honore suæ matris dedicaverat: et quod tres reges pagani ipsis duodecim, ad eorum sustenementum, duodecim portiones terræ dederunt.” Indeque Malmesburiensis: “ Duodecim discipulis sanctorum Philippi et Jacobi anno Dominicæ Incarnationis LXIII. in Britanniam venientibus, tres reges licet pagani XII. portiones terræ contulerunt: unde adhuc nomen XII. hidarum perseverat.” Hæc ille in libro de antiquitate Glastoniensis ecclesiæ: ubi XII. harum hidarum metas cum locis præcipuis quæ intra earum limites continentur, diligenter describit. Earundem etiam in libro censuali Guilielmi I. Anglorum regis, qui Domesday appellatur, ejusmodi fit mentio. “ Ecclesia Glastingebury habet in ipsa villa XII. hydas quæ nunquam geldaverunt.”
mt_english: Thomas Scropus, formerly bishop of Dromore in Ireland, also reports the same things concerning the arrival of Joseph, in chapter seven of the book he wrote "On the Antiquity of the Carmelite Order". And Thomas Harfeldius, in his "Breviary of the Kings of the English": where he says that Faganus and Duvianus (or Deruvianus), in the time of King Lucius, found on the island of Avalon "an ancient church built by the disciples of Christ, with ancient writings recording how, when the holy apostles were dispersed to preach, Saint Philip, coming into France, sent twelve of his disciples into Britain; over whom he also placed Joseph of Arimathea." And indeed there is still extant an epistle forged by the monks of Glastonbury in the name of our great Patrick (this is the charter of Saint Patrick, cited above by William of Malmesbury) in which he is introduced discussing the origin of the church which was called Ealdcirc by the Anglo-Saxons, that is, the old church, as follows: "The brothers showed me the writings of Saints Phaganus and Deruvianus: in which it was contained that twelve disciples of Saints Philip and James had built that same old church in honor of our aforementioned advocate, the Blessed Virgin Mary, through the instruction of the blessed archangel Gabriel. And moreover, that the Lord had dedicated the same church from heaven in honor of his mother: and that three pagan kings gave to those twelve, for their support, twelve portions of land." And from this Malmesbury writes: "When twelve disciples of Saints Philip and James came to Britain in the year of the Lord's Incarnation 63, three kings, although pagans, bestowed twelve portions of land: whence the name of the Twelve Hides still persists."
