latin: In hoc ergo casu bene potest probari hæc negativa per scripturam contrariam. Continetur enim in floribus sanctorum, sub legenda Jacobi minoris, contrarium. Hoc legitur quoque quod Titus intrans Hierusalem, quemdam murum densissimum vidit, ipsumque perforari jussit: et intus quendam senem repererunt, qui dixit se esse Joseph ab Arimathia, et se ibidem esse inclusum a Judæis quia Christum sepelisset, et quod usque ad tempus istud cœlesti cibo sit pastus. In evangelio tamen Nicodemi dicitur, quod Christus eum liberavit post resurrectionem suam, et in Arimathiam duxit. Potest autem dici quod eductus cum a prædicatione non cessaret, iterum sit ab ipsis Judæis inclusus. Hæc ubi supra. Cum ergo Joseph fuerit incarceratus tanto tempore apud Jerusalem, impossibile est eum fuisse in Anglia, cum sit magna distantia.
mt_english: In this case, therefore, this negative can well be proved by contrary writing. For the contrary is contained in the *Flowers of the Saints*, under the legend of James the Less. This is also read, that Titus, entering Jerusalem, saw a certain very thick wall, and ordered it to be broken through: and inside they found a certain old man, who said that he was Joseph of Arimathea, and that he had been enclosed there by the Jews because he had buried Christ, and that up to that time he had been fed with heavenly food. In the *Gospel of Nicodemus*, however, it is said that Christ freed him after his resurrection, and led him into Arimathea. But it can be said that, having been brought out, since he did not cease from preaching, he was again enclosed by the Jews themselves. These things are as above. Since, therefore, Joseph was imprisoned for so long a time at Jerusalem, it is impossible that he was in England, since the distance is great.
baker_ref: ). In this case, therefore, this negative can well be proved by contrary writings. For the contrary is contained in the Flowers of the Saints, under the Legend of James the Less. "Here it is also read that Titus entering into Jerusalem, saw that a certain wall was very thick, and ordered it to be pierced: and within they discovered a certain old man, who said he was Joseph of Arimathea, and that he had been imprisoned in that place by the Jews on account of his having buried Christ, and that even to that time he had been nourished on heavenly food. "Nevertheless, in the Gospel of Nicodemus it is said that Christ liberated him after his resurrection and conducted him into Arimathea. But it may be said that though released, when he ceased not to preach, he was imprisoned a second time by the Jews themselves. See as to this above. When, therefore, Joseph was imprisoned at such a time at Jerusalem it is impossible for him to have been in England, at so great a distance.

latin: III. Potest dici, quod licet hoc fuisset verum, (quod tamen non fuit) non sequitur ergo quod totum solium illud suscepit fidem. IV. Dicitur, dato illo quod negatur, adhuc tamen Hispani primo susceperunt fidem, quod probatur, quia Jacobus martyrium subiit vivente Petro. Scriptum est enin de Herode, quod occidit Jacobum gladio, et apposuit ut apprehenderet Petrum, Actuum capite duodecimo. Sed constat, quod Petrus passus est sub Nerone.
mt_english: III. It can be said that even if this had been true (which, however, it was not), it does not therefore follow that that entire realm received the faith. IV. It is said, granting what is denied, that the Spaniards nevertheless first received the faith, which is proved because James suffered martyrdom while Peter was living. For it is written concerning Herod, that he killed James with the sword, and proceeded to arrest Peter, in Acts 12. But it is certain that Peter suffered under Nero.
baker_ref: III. "It may be said, that even though this t (translated ). Or in the Acts of Pilate in Gregory of Tours. histor., lib. 1, cap. 20. were true (which, nevertheless, was not) it does not follow that that whole dominion received the faith. IV. "It is still affirmed, moreover, granted that which is denied, the Spanish first received the faith, which is proved, because James suffered martyrdom in the life of Peter. For it is written of Herod, that he slew James with the sword, and had the intention to apprehend Peter, Chapter XII of the Acts. But it is well known that Peter suffered under Nero.

latin: Nero autem fuit prope annum Domini LIV. et Titus fuit prope annum Domini LXXX. Jam certum est quod si Joseph fuisset in Anglia, hoo fuisset postquam de carcere fuisset liberatus per Titum, et sic post octogesimum annum a nativitate Domini: et Jacobus mortuus est ante Neronem pluribus annis, quasi prope quadragesimum annum a nativitate Domini. Et Hispania suscepit fidem a Jaoobo, vivente eo, vel statim in sepultura ejus; ut supra dixi. Ergo Hispania est in fide antiquior." Hæc ad patres Basileensis concilii Alphonsus Garsias: in quibus quædam sunt levia admodum, nonnulla etiam oppido ridicula.
mt_english: "Now Nero was around A.D. 54, and Titus was around A.D. 80. Now it is certain that if Joseph had been in England, this would have been after he had been freed from prison by Titus, and thus after the eightieth year from the birth of the Lord; and James died many years before Nero, around the fortieth year from the birth of the Lord. And Spain received the faith from James, while he was living, or immediately upon his burial, as I said above. Therefore Spain is older in the faith." Alfonso Garcia addressed these things to the fathers of the Council of Basel: in which some things are quite trivial, and some even completely ridiculous.
baker_ref: Nero, moreover, was about the year of Our Lord 54 and Titus about the year 80. Now it is certain that if Joseph were in England, this was after he was liberated from prison by Titus, and thus after the 80th year from the Nativity of Our Lord: and James died many years before Nero, about the 40th year from the Lord's nativity. "And Spain received the faith from James, in his lifetime, or immediately on his burial; as above stated. Therefore Spain is the more ancient in the faith." Thus Alphonsus Garcias to the Fathers at the Council of Basle: wherein some things are wholly trivial, not a few exceedingly ridiculous.

latin: Ad primam ejus responsionem quod attinet: historias et scripta antiqua Josephi ad Britannos legationem confirmantia, quanta potuimus diligentia superius collegimus, atque in medium produximus. Quibus jam addimus oratorum et legatorum regis Angliæ, in hac ipsa synodo propositam assertionem. "Certum est in Anglia reperiri in libris antiquissimis et archivis, præcipue in archivis abbatiæ notabilis Glastonensis, diocesis Bathoniensis; quod Joseph ab Arimathia cum duodecim sociis, aut ex persecutione Herodiana, vel præsidum Romanorum in Judæa, ad Angliam vectus est. Ibidem, quæ de Christo viderat et audierat prædicavit, et prædicando plures convertit; convertendo, multa et infinita sibi, ab illis quos converterat ad fidem collata, conquæsivit; conquæsita postea templo Christo per eum erecto reliquit: (et hoc, tempore quo Petrus in Antiochia prædicavit fidem:) quod templum a Joseph erectum, in locum religiosum et abbatialem dignitatem translatum est, et laus Christi per notabile monasterium præservatur ad præsens."
mt_english: As for his first response: I have collected above, with as much diligence as I could, the histories and ancient writings confirming the mission of Joseph to the Britons, and I have brought them forward. To which I now add the assertion proposed by the orators and legates of the king of England in this very synod: "It is certain that it is found in England in the most ancient books and archives, especially in the archives of the notable abbey of Glastonbury, in the diocese of Bath, that Joseph of Arimathea with twelve companions, either from the Herodian persecution or that of the Roman governors in Judea, sailed to England. There, he preached what he had seen and heard concerning Christ, and by preaching he converted many; by converting, he acquired many and infinite things bestowed upon him by those whom he had converted to the faith; the things acquired he afterwards left to a temple erected by him to Christ (and this, at the time when Peter preached the faith in Antioch): which temple erected by Joseph was translated into a religious place and abbatial dignity, and the praise of Christ is preserved by a notable monastery to the present."
baker_ref: In regard to his first reply: the histories and ancient writings corroborating the mission of Joseph to the British, we have brought together above with as much diligence as we could, and have produced in evidence. To which we now add the declaration put forward in that Council by the Ambassadors and Legates of the King of England: “Certain it is that in England are to be found in the most ancient books and archives, principally in the archives of the notable Abbey of Glaston, in the diocese of Bath; that Joseph of Arimathea with twelve companions, either in consequence of the persecution of Herod, or of the Roman Governors of Judea, sailed to England. There he preached what he had seen and heard concerning Christ, and by his preaching converted many; and converting them he acquired for himself an infinite number of things collected by those he had converted to the faith; these acquisitions he afterwards left to a Church erected by his means to Christ (and this at the time that Peter preached the faith at Antioch ): which Church, erected by Joseph, has developed into a place of religion and of the dignity of an Abbey, and by means of a notable monastery the praise of Christ is preserved to the present time."

latin: Probabilitatem contrariam, quam secundo loco urget, negamus omnino esse probabilem. Neque enim aliquem hodie, si Thomam Dempsterum exceperis, tam stulte credulum esse existimamus, cui absurdissimum illud commentum, de Josepho muro incluso, probabile videri possit: et de legendæ aureæ authore Jacobo de Voragine, ex cujus areolis fœtidi isti sanctorum flores sunt decerpti, in ipsa Hispania a Ludovico Vive et Melchiore Cano jamdudum lata est sententia; ferrei oris eum virum fuisse, atque plumbei cordis.
mt_english: I entirely deny that the contrary probability, which he urges in the second place, is probable. For I do not think that anyone today, if you except Thomas Dempster, is so foolishly credulous that this most absurd fiction about Joseph being enclosed in a wall could seem probable to him; and concerning Jacobus de Voragine, the author of the *Golden Legend*, from whose garden beds those fetid flowers of the saints were plucked, a judgment was long ago passed in Spain itself by Ludovicus Vives and Melchior Cano: that he was a man of an iron mouth and a leaden heart.
baker_ref: We entirely deny that the contrary probability which he urges in the second place, is probable. Nor do we think that anyone to -day, if Thomas Dempster be excepted, " is so foolishly credulous u Apparat, ad histor. Scot, lib. 1, cap. 7, pag. 27; Vid. Melchiorem Inchofer, de veritate epistolae B. Mariae ad Messanenses, cap. 13, pag. 71, 72. as to regard as probable this very absurd fabrication concerning Joseph of Arimathea shut up in a wall; and concerning the author of the "Golden Legend", Jacobo de Voragine," from whose garden plots these fetid Flowers of the Saints are gathered, in Spain itself the opinion is expressed now and has been for a long time. past by Ludovicus Vives and Melchiore Cano that that man was brazen of speech and leaden of heart.

latin: Tertium illud, quod totum Britanniæ regnum Josephi ministerio fidem non susceperit; verum quidem est, sed ad rem non pertinet. Nam nec totum regnum Hispaniæ a Jacobo conversum fuisse ipsi Hispani dicent; nec integra regna ab ullo apostolorum Christiana facta esse constat: et de antiquitate, non de universalitate susceptionis fidei instituta est quæstio.
mt_english: The third point, that the whole kingdom of Britain did not receive the faith through the ministry of Joseph, is indeed true, but it is irrelevant. For the Spaniards themselves will not say that the whole kingdom of Spain was converted by James; nor is it established that entire kingdoms were made Christian by any of the apostles: and the question raised concerns the antiquity, not the universality, of the reception of the faith.
baker_ref: As to the third point, that the whole of the realm of Britain did not receive the faith by the ministry of Joseph, it is true enough but it is not relevant to the issue. For neither do the Spanish themselves say that the whole kingdom of Spain was converted by James; nor is it established that whole kingdoms were made Christian by any one of the Apostles: and, moreover, the question at issue concerns the antiquity, not the universality, of the reception of the faith.

latin: Quartum vero et postremum, partim incertis, partim falsis nititur fundamentis. Jacobi prædicationem in Hispania, inter incerta posuit Rodericus Ximenius Toletanus archiepiscopus, in concertatione quam anno MCCXV. in Lateranensi concilio cum præsule Compostellano de primatu habuit. Ejus verba, a Garsia Loaisa e libro MS. bibliothecæ Toletanæ edita, hæc sunt. “ Si inducat (Compostellanus) primam divini verbi promulgationem, et plurimorum conversionem ad fidem Christi in Hispania (per Jacobum factam:) qui divinam paginam noverunt, testimonium perhibeant. Ego tantum legi, datam ei fuisse potestatem prædicandi in Hispania: sed interim, cum per Judæam et Samariam divinam legem seminaret, sub Herode Hierosolymis truncato capite exhalavit animam, et Domino reddidit. Quomodo ergo ibi prædicavit, quo nondum ingressus est? aut sine prædicatione, quos, obsecro, convertit ad Dominum?” Nec ex parte altera certum est, quantumvis id ita esse affirmet Alphonsus, “ quod si Joseph fuisset in Anglia, hoc fuisset postquam de carcere liberatus fuisset per Titum, et sic post octuagesimum annum a nativitate Domini.” A Tito enim, anno æræ Christianæ (non octogesimo sed) septuagesimo eversam esse Hierosolymam certum est: quæ vero de Josepho Arimathæensi tunc per eum liberato pro certis assumuntur, nugæ sunt nugerrimæ.
mt_english: The fourth and final point rests partly on uncertain, partly on false foundations. Rodrigo Jiménez, archbishop of Toledo, placed the preaching of James in Spain among uncertain things, in the dispute which he had concerning the primacy with the prelate of Compostela at the Lateran Council in the year 1215. His words, published by García Loaysa from a manuscript book of the library of Toledo, are these: "If he (the prelate of Compostela) adduces the first promulgation of the divine word, and the conversion of very many to the faith of Christ in Spain (accomplished by James): let those who know the divine page bear witness. I have only read that the power of preaching in Spain was given to him: but in the meantime, while he was sowing the divine law through Judea and Samaria, he breathed out his soul, his head having been cut off under Herod at Jerusalem, and returned it to the Lord. How therefore did he preach there, where he had not yet entered? Or without preaching, whom, I ask, did he convert to the Lord?" Nor on the other hand is it certain, however much Alfonso may affirm it to be so, "that if Joseph had been in England, this would have been after he had been freed from prison by Titus, and thus after the eightieth year from the birth of the Lord." For it is certain that Jerusalem was overthrown by Titus in the seventieth (not the eightieth) year of the Christian era: but the things which are assumed as certain concerning Joseph of Arimathea being freed by him at that time are the most trifling nonsense.
baker_ref: As to the fourth and last point, this rests partly upon doubtful, and partly upon false, premises. Rodericus Ximensis, Archbishop of Toledo, accounted the preaching of James in Spain as doubtful, in the controversy which he had in the year 1215, in the Lateran Council with the Prefect of Compostella, concerning the w Jacob. Januens, in legenda S. Jacobi minoris. * Vives, de causis corrupt. artium. lib. 2. y Can. de locis Theolog. lib. 11., cap. 6. primacy. His words, published by Garsia Loaisa from the MS. book of the Toledo Library, are: "If he (Compostellanus ) brings forward the first promulgation of the Divine Word and the conversion of very many to the faith of Christ in Spain (accomplished by James ), let them who are acquainted with Holy Writ produce the evidence. I only know that the opportunity was given him of preaching in Spain: but, in the meantime, while sowing the Divine Word through Judea and Samaria, he was decapitated under Herod at Jerusalem and giving up the Ghost, rendered it unto his Lord. How, therefore, did he preach there where he had not been at all? or whom, pray, without preaching, did he convert to the Lord?” Nor on the other hand is it certain, however much Alphonsus may affirm it to be so, "That if Joseph was in England, it was after he had been liberated from prison by Titus, and so after the 80th year from the Lord's Nativity. For it is certain that Jerusalem was destroyed by Titus in the 70th year (not the 80th ) of the Christian era: in fact, that which is assumed as certain concerning Joseph of Arimathea being liberated by him is an idle tale of the most frivolous character. z Collect. Concil. Hispan, a Loaisa edit., pag. 291; et Concil. edit. Colon.

latin: Guilielmus quidem Eysengreineus ex annalibus Anglorum narrat eum “ post urbis Hierosolymæ destructionem apostolis adhæsisse; atque hoc pacto jam senem in Britanniam profectum, in urbe Wellia Christum prædicavisse.” Sed temporis illam circumstantiam in nullis Anglorum annalibus expressam reperit. Glastonienses, et Malmesburiensis monachus in secundo Eulogii sui libro, Josephi adventum ad annum Christi LXIII. referunt: quem ab assumptione beatæ virginis XV. fuisse tradunt.
mt_english: William Eisengrein indeed relates from the annals of the English that he "joined the apostles after the destruction of the city of Jerusalem; and in this manner, having set out for Britain already an old man, preached Christ in the city of Wells." But he found this circumstance of time expressed in no annals of the English. The monks of Glastonbury, and the monk of Malmesbury in the second book of his "Eulogium", assign the arrival of Joseph to the year of Christ 63, which they record to have been the fifteenth year from the assumption of the Blessed Virgin.
baker_ref: an. 1618, tom. 2, part 2, pag. 317, 318. Vide Baron. annal., tom. 9., an. 816., sec. 49, 50, 51, 52, et bibliothec. Floriacens. Joannis Certainly William Eysengreineusª in his annals of the English relates that he "after the destruction of Jerusalem attached himself to the Apostles: and that, by agreement, he proceeded to Britain when he was now old, and preached Christ in the city of Wells." But in no English annals does he find that express circumstance as to time. The Glastonians, and the monk of Malmesbury in the second book of his Eulogy, refer the coming of Joseph to the year of Christ 63: which they propound as the fifteenth from the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin.

latin: Oratores Angli, ut diximus, in Basileensi hoc concilio, templum a Josepho in Britannia erectum asserunt, “ tempore quo Petrus in Antiochia prædicavit fidem :” et in Constantiensi, “ statim post passionem Christi” eundem Britanniam ingressum esse, et populos ad fidem convertisse defendunt. Quod et cum ipsius Josephi ætate, qui Domino passionem adeunte inter Judæos senator honoratus fuerat, et cum iis quæ initio ex Gilda de tempore summo Tiberii Cæsaris produximus, bene quadrat.
mt_english: The English orators, as I have said, at this Council of Basel, assert that a church was erected by Joseph in Britain "at the time when Peter preached the faith in Antioch:" and at the Council of Constance, they maintain that "immediately after the passion of Christ" he entered Britain and converted the peoples to the faith. This accords well both with the age of Joseph himself, who, when the Lord underwent his passion, had been an honored senator among the Jews, and with those things which I produced at the beginning from Gildas concerning the latter time of Tiberius Caesar.
baker_ref: The English Ambassadors, as we have said, claim in this Council of Basle that a Church had been erected by Joseph in Britain " at the time when Peter preached the faith in Antioch ": and in the Council of Constance, they maintained that "immediately after the Passion of Christ " he entered Britain and converted the people to the faith. Which well agrees both with the age of Joseph himself, who when the Lord was entering upon his Passion, had been an honoured senator among the Jews, and with those things which at the commencement we produced from a Eysengrein. cent. 1, part 6, distinct. 6. b Mar.

latin: Johannes enim Hardingius indignus est, cujus hic ulla habeatur ratio : qui Josephum per ipsos quadraginta duos a Christi morte annos, non quidem in muro, sed in Caiphæ carcere detentum, sine omni cibo et potu vixisse ; deinde a Vespasiano liberatum, et in Britanniam anno Christi LXXVI. perductum, ibique regi Arvirago et conjugi ipsius Genissæ (quæ Claudii imperatoris filia fuisse fingitur) commendatum fuisse fabulatur. Johannes Balæus, Ossoriensis aliquando apud Hibernos episcopus, eodem illo anno ex vita hac migrasse eum scribit. “ In sancta senectute (inquit) Josephus inter discipulos tandem quietam morte carnis dormitionem accepit, in Avalonica solitudine sepultus, anno a Christi incarnatione LXXVI. Mario regnante in Britannia. Postea translatum est ejus corpus ad Glasconiense monachorum collegium, et in pretiosa theca repositum. Neque desunt (inquit ille) qui ex conjecturis habeant, contexuisse illum ad ecclesias Britannorum epistolas quasdam.” Quam conjecturam ut verisimiliorem redderet Guilielmus Eysengreineus, ne a præsente ad præsentes literæ scriptæ putarentur, “ reliquisse insulam et, ut renovaret sui memoriam, scripsisse epistolam ad Britannos” illum fingit: Anglorum hic quoque citatis annalibus ; in quibus tamen neque Britanniam eum reliquisse, neque ejusmodi aliquam epistolam scripsisse, neque alibi quam Glastoniæ mortuum et sepultum fuisse, uspiam traditum invenimus.
mt_english: For John Harding is unworthy of any consideration here, who fables that Joseph, detained for forty-two years from the death of Christ, not indeed in a wall, but in the prison of Caiaphas, lived without any food or drink; and that he was then freed by Vespasian, brought to Britain in the year of Christ 76, and there commended to King Arviragus and his wife Genissa (who is imagined to have been the daughter of the emperor Claudius). John Bale, sometime bishop of Ossory among the Irish, writes that he departed from this life in that same year. "In holy old age," he says, "Joseph at last received a quiet sleep in the death of the flesh among the disciples, being buried in the solitude of Avalon, in the year from the incarnation of Christ 76, while Marius was reigning in Britain. Afterwards his body was translated to the college of monks at Glastonbury, and laid to rest in a precious shrine. Nor are there lacking," he says, "those who hold by conjecture that he composed certain epistles to the churches of the Britons." To render this conjecture more probable, Wilhelm Eisengrein, lest letters should be thought to have been written by one present to those present, imagines that he "left the island and, to renew the memory of himself, wrote an epistle to the Britons," citing here also the annals of the English; in which, however, I find it nowhere recorded that he either left Britain, or wrote any such epistle, or died and was buried anywhere other than at Glastonbury.
baker_ref: cap. 15., ver. 43. evoxýμwv Bovλeuròs quod a vulgato interprete, nobilis decurio, redditur, de quo videndus commentarius B. Hieronymi in Matth., cap. 27., et Ludovici de Dieu V.C. in Marc., cap. 15. Et. H. Grotii, in Matth., cap. 27., ver. 57. Qui apud Plinium Secundum, lib. 10, epist. 113. Buleutae in Rescripto Trajani, epist. 114. decuriones appellantur. Gildas concerning the last days of Tiberias Cæsar. For John Harding does not deserve that any respect should be paid to him here: who pretends that Joseph for these forty -two years from the death of Christ, lived, not indeed in a wall, but detained in the prison of Caiaphas, without food or drink: that then he was liberated by Vespasian and brought over to Britain in the year of Christ 76 and that there he was commended to the king Arviragus and his wife Genissa (who is represented as being the daughter of the Emperor Claudius ). John Bale, sometime Bishop of Ossory in Ireland, writes that he departed this life in that same year. " In sainted old age (he says )ª Joseph at length in the midst of his disciples by the death of the body gained the sleep of peace, being buried in the solitude of Avalon in the year 76 from Christ's Incarnation and in the reign of Marius in Britain. Afterwards his body was translated to the College of the Monks of Glaston and enclosed in a casket of great price. Nor are there wanting (says he) those who from conjectures maintain that he composed a certain Epistle to the British churches." Which conjecture William Eysengreineus, that he might render it more probable, and that the epistle might not be regarded as written by one present to those present, pretends that he " had left the island and in order to keep his memory green, had written an Epistle to the British": here, too, with a quotation from the Annals of the English: in which, however, we find it nowhere stated that he had either left Britain or written any letter of the kind or had died and been buried elsewhere than at Glaston.

latin: Extat vetustus catalogus sanctorum in Anglia sepultorum Saxonice scriptus, ac Latine, a Gotcelino Bertiniano monacho Cantuariensi, Anselmi archiepiscopi diebus editus: et de reliquis in Glastoniensi monasterio repositis libellus alter, Henrici III. Anglorum regis temporibus exaratus. In neutro vero Josephi ulla occurrit mentio.
mt_english: There is an ancient catalogue of saints buried in England, written in Saxon, and published in Latin by Goscelin of Saint-Bertin, a monk of Canterbury, in the days of Archbishop Anselm; and another short book concerning the relics deposited in the monastery of Glastonbury, composed in the time of Henry III, king of the English. But in neither does any mention of Joseph occur.
baker_ref: There exists a very ancient register of Saints buried in England, written in the Saxon tongue, and in Latin, by Gotcelinus Bertinianus, a monk of Canterbury, published in the days of Archbishop Anselm: and another book concerning the relics preserved at the Monastery of Glaston, discovered in the times of Henry III, King of England. In neither, indeed, does any mention occur of Joseph.

latin: Anno demum MCCCXLV. a Johanne Blomæo Londinensi, cujusdam revelationis sibi factæ prætextu, ab Edvardo III. licentia quærendi corpus Josephi ab Arimathia impetrata est: quam, ex archivis regiis in arce Londinensi asservatis a me descriptam, lectori communicare non gravabor.
mt_english: Finally, in the year 1345, John Blome of London, on the pretext of a certain revelation made to him, obtained from Edward III a license to search for the body of Joseph of Arimathea. I will not hesitate to share this with the reader, having copied it from the royal archives preserved in the Tower of London.
baker_ref: At length, in the year 1345, a license was procured from Edward III by John Blome of London on the pretext of a certain revelation made to him, to seek for the body of Joseph of Arimathea: which, as transcribed by me from the royal archives preserved in the Tower of London, I do not think it amiss to communicate to the reader: e Septoniæ enim sepultum fuisse (ea Dorsettensium Shaftesburia est) per errorem scriptum legitur in Jo.

latin: “Rex omnibus ad quos, &c. salutem. Supplicavit nobis Johannes Blome de London, ut cum sibi (sicut asserit) divinitus sit injunctum, ut venerandum corpus decurionis nobilis Josephi ab Arimathia, quod infra septa monasterii Glastoniensis in Christo quiescit humatum, et est ad honorem et multorum ædificationem his temporibus revelandum, quærat donec inveniat diligenter. Et quia in quibusdam antiquis scripturis dicitur contineri corpus ejus ibidem fuisse sepultum. Nos, si sit ita, desiderantes monumentum ejus, et venerandas ipsius reliquias, qui redemptori nostro morienti tantum exhibebat pietatis et humanitatis obsequium, corpus ejus de cruce deponendo, et illud in monumento suo novo ponendo, devotis honoribus prævenire; et sperantes nobis et toti regno nostro ex revelatione prædicta gratiam uberiorem provenire: concessimus et licentiam dedimus (quantum in nobis est) eidem Johanni quod ipse infra præcinctum dicti monasterii fodere, et illas prætiosas reliquias juxta injunctionem et revelationem sibi factam quærere valeat in locis ubi melius viderit expedire: dum tamen absque damno dilectorum nobis in Christo, abbatis et conventus dicti monasterii, et ruina ecclesiæ et domorum suarum ibidem id fieri valeat; et quod ad id ipsorum abbatis et conventus licentiam habeat et assensum. In cujus, &c. Teste Rege PER IPSUM REGEM.
mt_english: "The King to all to whom, etc., greeting. John Blome of London has petitioned us that, since (as he asserts) it has been divinely enjoined upon him, he may diligently search until he finds the venerable body of the noble decurion Joseph of Arimathea, which rests buried in Christ within the bounds of the monastery of Glastonbury, and is to be revealed in these times for the honor and edification of many. And because it is said to be contained in certain ancient writings that his body was buried there, we—if it be so—desiring to anticipate with devout honors his monument and the venerable relics of him who showed such pious and humane devotion to our dying Redeemer by taking his body down from the cross and placing it in his own new tomb, and hoping that more abundant grace may come to us and to our whole kingdom from the aforesaid revelation, have granted and given license (as far as lies in our power) to the same John that he may dig within the precinct of the said monastery and seek those precious relics according to the injunction and revelation made to him, in the places where he shall see it most expedient: provided, however, that this can be done without damage to our beloved in Christ, the abbot and convent of the said monastery, and without the ruin of their church and houses there; and that for this he has the license and assent of the abbot and convent themselves. In witness of which, etc. Witness the King, BY THE KING HIMSELF."

We, if it be so, being desirous of a memorial of him and of shewing all fitting honours to the venerable remains of him who shewed for our dying Redeemer such homage of piety and humanity in removing His body from the Cross and placing it in his own new tomb; and trusting to produce for ourselves and for our whole nation the greater favour: Concede and grant license (so far as in us lies ) to the same John to dig beneath the precincts of the said Monastery and that it be lawful for him to seek those precious remains according to the charge and revelation made to him in such places as he may think fit: Provided nevertheless that it can be done without detriment to our well beloved in Christ,the Abbot and Chapter of the said Monastery, and without damage totheir Church and dwellings and tothis end he should have the license and assent of the Abbot and Chapter themselves.

latin: " Et inter cætera memini me vidisse Glasconiæ in cruce lapidea, quæ sub regina Elizabetha subversa fuit, laminam æneam in qua scribebatur, Josephum ab Arimathæa trigesimo anno post passionem Christi venisse in Britanniam cum undecim vel duodecim sociis, permissumque ei ab Arvirago rege, Glasconiæ quæ tunc erat insula dicta Avalonia, habitare, tanquam solitarios viros et simplices : et quod attulerit secum duo vasa argentea non grandia, in quibus erat de sanguine et aqua sacratissima, quæ profluxerat de latere Christi mortui. Crux autem ista erecta est ante multos annos ad denotandam longitudinem sacelli ab eodem sancto Josepho ex vimineis cratibus constructi in honorem beatissimæ virginis; deducta scilicet linea recta a medio illius crucis ad latus sacelli postea lapidibus quadratis exædificati: sub qua item erat olim illud sacellum Sancti Josephi in crypta subterranea. Foris autem in muro hujus sacelli beatæ virginis erant in lapide sculpta vetustissimis literis hæc duo verba, Jesus, Maria. Et confirmant antiqua arma Glasconiensis monasterii, quæ sunt hujusmodi: Scutum album in quo per longum erigitur stipes crucis viridis et nodosæ, et de latere ad latus extenduntur brachia seu rami crucis stipiti consimilia.
mt_english: 'And among other things I remember seeing at Glastonbury on a stone cross, which was overthrown under Queen Elizabeth, a brass plate on which it was written, that Joseph of Arimathea came to Britain in the thirtieth year after the passion of Christ with eleven or twelve companions, and that he was permitted by King Arviragus to dwell at Glastonbury, which was then an island called Avalonia, as solitary and simple men: and that he brought with him two small silver vessels, in which was some of the most sacred blood and water that had flowed from the side of the dead Christ. Moreover, that cross was erected many years ago to mark the length of the chapel constructed by the same St. Joseph from woven wattles in honor of the most blessed Virgin; a straight line being drawn, namely, from the middle of that cross to the side of the chapel afterwards built of squared stones: under which also was formerly that chapel of St. Joseph in a subterranean crypt. But outside on the wall of this chapel of the blessed Virgin these two words were carved in stone in very ancient letters, Jesus, Maria. And the ancient arms of the monastery of Glastonbury confirm this, which are of this kind: A white shield in which lengthwise is erected the trunk of a green and knotty cross, and from side to side extend the arms or branches of the cross similar to the trunk.'
baker_ref: "And, among other things, I remember to have seen at Glasconia on a stone cross, which was overturned under Queen Elizabeth, a brass tablet on which was inscribed, that Joseph of Arimathea came to Britain in the thirtieth year after the Passion of Christ with eleven or twelve companions, and that he was allowed by King Arviragus to dwell at Glasconia which was then an island called Avalonia, as solitary and simple men: and that he brought with him two silver vases of no great size in which was some of the most holy blood and water which had flowed from the side of the dead Christ. Moreover this same cross was erected many years before to denote the length of the chapel constructed by the aforesaid St. Joseph of willow wattles in honour of the Blessed Virgin: to wit, with a straight line drawn from the middle of the Cross to the side of the Chapel that was afterwards built of squared stones: under which hvid. supr., pag. 31, et 37. was also once the Chapel of St. Joseph in a subterranean crypt. Moreover outside in the wall of this Chapel of the Blessed Virgin there were carved in stone in characters of great age these two words, JESUS, MARIA. And the ancient arms of the Monastery of Glasconia confirm this, which are as follows: A white shield on which longways is erected the shaft of a green and knotty cross and from side to side are stretched arms or branches of the cross similar to the shaft.
